title: Decoding
oneLine: Turn the model's next-token distribution into actual generated text.

paras: A language model outputs a probability distribution over the next token. Decoding is the policy that picks one — and that choice shapes everything about the output. Always taking the argmax (greedy) is fluent but repetitive; sampling adds variety but can wander.
Temperature sharpens or flattens the distribution; top-k and top-p (nucleus) clip the long tail so you sample only from plausible tokens; beam search keeps several candidate continuations at once.
Temperature T rescales the logits before the softmax — low T concentrates probability on the top tokens, high T spreads it out:
sections.texNote: T -> 0 recovers greedy argmax; T = 1 is the model's raw distribution.

sections.code:
import numpy as np

def sample(logits, T=1.0, top_p=0.9):
    z = logits / T
    p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
    order = np.argsort(p)[::-1]                 # nucleus: keep smallest
    keep = order[np.cumsum(p[order]) <= top_p]  # set with mass >= top_p
    if len(keep) == 0: keep = order[:1]
    p2 = p[keep] / p[keep].sum()
    return np.random.choice(keep, p=p2)
sections.caption: Temperature reshapes the distribution; top-p trims the tail before sampling.

takeaways: Decoding is a separate policy on top of the model's distribution — it controls the style of the output.
Temperature trades determinism for diversity; top-k / top-p remove implausible tokens.
Greedy is just temperature -> 0; beam search searches several continuations at once.
